questions.question: At the bedside, the donation number on an RBC unit does not match the compatibility tag. What should the RN do?
choices: Do not start the transfusion and contact the transfusion service
Start slowly because the client name matches
Ask the client whether the unit looks correct
Change the tag to match the unit number
questions.explanation: Any discrepancy in the bedside verification stops the process. The unit must remain disconnected until the mismatch is resolved through the approved transfusion-service process.

questions.question: Ten minutes after an RBC transfusion begins, a client reports chills and new low-back pain. Which action is the priority?
choices: Stop the transfusion immediately
Give an antipyretic and continue
Increase the rate to finish the unit
Document the symptoms after the unit is complete
questions.explanation: Chills and back pain may signal an acute hemolytic or other serious reaction. Stop the transfusion first, then support ABCs, keep access available with new compatible tubing per protocol, verify identity, and notify the provider and blood bank.

questions.question: Which finding cluster most strongly suggests an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?
choices: Fever, flank pain, hypotension, and dark urine
Isolated mild itching without other symptoms
Gradual fatigue one month later
Hypertension, neck-vein distention, and peripheral edema
questions.explanation: Fever, pain, hypotension, and hemoglobinuria are urgent clues to intravascular hemolysis. Stop the transfusion and activate the reaction and emergency pathway.

questions.question: During an RBC transfusion, a client with heart failure develops dyspnea, crackles, hypertension, jugular venous distention, and a positive fluid balance. Which complication is most likely?
choices: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)
Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI)
Delayed hemolytic reaction
Isolated urticarial reaction
questions.explanation: The hydrostatic overload pattern—hypertension, venous distention, positive balance, and heart-failure risk—supports TACO. Stop the transfusion, support oxygenation, and follow the reaction protocol.

questions.question: A client develops acute hypoxemia and bilateral pulmonary edema during transfusion, but assessment does not show circulatory overload. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
choices: TRALI should be considered
TACO is proven because pulmonary edema is present
This cannot be transfusion related without hives
The transfusion should continue while awaiting imaging
questions.explanation: TRALI presents with acute hypoxemic lung injury and pulmonary edema without circulatory overload as the main explanation. Stop the transfusion and support oxygenation while notifying the provider and transfusion service.

questions.question: A stable client needs routine intravascular volume expansion but has no bleeding-related coagulation-factor deficiency. Which statement about plasma is correct?
choices: Plasma is not a routine general volume expander
Plasma is preferred because it contains no proteins
Plasma should replace all crystalloid therapy
Plasma is equivalent to a platelet transfusion
questions.explanation: Plasma supplies multiple coagulation proteins and should be matched to an appropriate hemostatic indication. It is not routine volume replacement or interchangeable with platelets.

questions.question: A bleeding client has critically low fibrinogen. Which blood component is specifically rich in fibrinogen?
choices: Cryoprecipitate
Packed red blood cells
Albumin
Washed platelets
questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate is a concentrated source of fibrinogen and may be ordered for clinically important hypofibrinogenemia. The exact product and dose follow laboratory findings and protocol.

questions.question: Which monitoring plan is most important during massive transfusion?
choices: Temperature, ionized calcium, potassium, acid–base status, coagulation, fibrinogen, platelets, bleeding, and perfusion
Hemoglobin alone after all products are complete
Daily weight as the only assessment
Skin testing for every transfused component
questions.explanation: Massive transfusion can cause hypothermia, citrate-related hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, acid–base changes, and coagulopathy. Continuous clinical assessment and repeated targeted labs guide resuscitation.

questions.question: Which action is appropriate while administering an RBC unit?
choices: Use approved filtered blood tubing and only a policy-approved compatible solution
Inject prescribed medication directly into the blood bag
Use an improvised heating pad to warm the unit
Share the blood line with any IV medication if the rate is slow
questions.explanation: Blood requires approved administration equipment and compatible solution. Medications are not added to the component, and only approved blood warmers are used for defined indications.

questions.question: Ten days after an RBC transfusion, a client reports fatigue and dark urine and has an unexpected hemoglobin decrease and jaundice. Which problem should the RN suspect?
choices: Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction
Immediate anaphylaxis
TACO
Simple dehydration only
questions.explanation: A delayed hemolytic reaction can emerge days to weeks after transfusion with falling hemoglobin, jaundice, dark urine, fatigue, or fever. The client needs prompt evaluation and preservation of antibody history.
